# Ethics Beyond Compliance {#sec-ethics}

In 2016 two researchers scraped some 70,000 profiles from the
dating site OkCupid and posted them to an open research
repository: usernames beside answers to intimate questions about
sexuality, drug use, and politics. Asked about consent, they
replied that the data were already public, which was true and
beside the point [@zimmer2016okcupid]. Every user had disclosed
each answer to an audience of their choosing; the release joined
the disclosures into one permanent, searchable file attached to
the names people use. No number in it was false, and no
regulation the researchers recognized stopped them. This chapter
is about failures of that kind, in which every rule is followed
and every reader is still misled or harmed, and about why the
statistician, not the institutional review board (IRB), is often
the last person who can stop them.

::: {.bookepigraph}

```{=latex}
\begin{flushright}\small
```
*The first principle is that you must not fool yourself, and
you are the easiest person to fool.*

[Richard P. Feynman]{.smallcaps}, *Cargo Cult Science* (1974)

## Compliance is a floor {#sec-ethics-floor}

The regulatory chapters of this book describe a floor. @sec-federal
covers what the funders require, @sec-deident what the Health
Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) Privacy Rule
requires, and @sec-cdisc what the Food and Drug Administration
requires. Clearing that floor is necessary for defensible practice
and nowhere near sufficient. The floor is written in terms of
*procedures*, and the failures that matter most are failures of
*inference*.

### Five failures and where each is caught

Five such failures recur in biomedical work, and they share a
structure: at no point does anyone state a falsehood. The data are
real, the computation is correct, the p-value is what the software
returned, the figure plots the numbers it claims to plot. The
misleading happens in the gap between what was computed and what
the reader concludes. @tbl-ethics-caught is the map for the rest of
the chapter: each failure enters the workflow at a different point,
so each is caught at a different point.

| Failure | Introduced at | Caught by |
|---|---|---|
| Aggregation harm | Data acquisition (@sec-acquisition) | Asking, before you assemble, whether the people in the data would be surprised |
| Causal overclaiming | The Results-to-Discussion transition | Reading your own discussion for causal verbs; peer review (@sec-communicating) |
| Visual misrepresentation | Figure construction (@sec-graphics) | Asking what the reader's eye is measuring |
| Overlapping-interval fallacy | Interpretation, and often the figure | Reporting the contrast, not the arms |
| Unrepresentative sample | Study design and recruitment; sometimes acquisition | Reporting who was sampled beside who the result is for; a proxy audit before a model acts |

: Where each failure enters the workflow and what catches it.
None is caught by a test suite, a lockfile, or a container.
{#tbl-ethics-caught}

The last line of the caption is the point of the chapter. The
infrastructure of this book is orthogonal to whether an analysis
misleads: reproducibility guarantees that a wrong conclusion can be
regenerated exactly.

### You are the last person who can catch it

The clinical collaborator cannot evaluate whether the confidence
interval supports the sentence in the abstract; that is why they
have you. The reviewer may or may not look, and the reader
certainly will not. When the press release says 'exercise prevents
cancer' and your analysis found an association in an observational
cohort of volunteers, you are not a bystander to that sentence. You
are its last opportunity.

Distortion is usually accidental, which does not make it harmless.
Almost nobody sets out to deceive with a truncated axis; they set
out to make the effect visible, and a truncated axis makes it
visible. Intent is not the standard. The standard is what a
competent reader would conclude.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A paper reports an observational study. The IRB
approved it, the data are de-identified under Safe Harbor, the Data
Management and Sharing Plan (DMSP) is in place, the code is on
Zenodo with a digital object identifier (DOI), and every number is
correctly computed. The abstract concludes that the intervention
'reduces 30-day readmission'. Has anything gone wrong?

**Answer.** Yes, and nothing in the compliance apparatus was built
to catch it. What is wrong is a verb: an observational design
licenses 'was associated with lower readmission', not 'reduces'.
The distinction is not pedantry. A guideline committee or a health
system deciding where to spend money will act on 'reduces', and the
evidence does not support the action. Reproducibility, compliance,
and correct computation are each necessary and jointly
insufficient; only the analyst can close the gap.
:::

## Professional standards and misconduct {#sec-ethics-standards}

The profession has written its obligations down. The American
Statistical Association's *Ethical Guidelines for Statistical
Practice*, approved by its Board in February 2022
[@asa2022ethical], apply to anyone who practices statistics,
whatever their title. They are organized as eight principles,
and most of this book's habits are instances of one of them
(@tbl-ethics-asa).

| ASA principle | What it asks of you | Where this book practices it |
|---|---|---|
| A. Professional integrity and accountability | Methods you can defend; honesty about limitations | Every Verification callout |
| B. Integrity of data and methods | Report data and methods so others can assess them; disclose what you removed | @sec-analysis-plan, @sec-missing |
| C. Responsibilities to stakeholders | Clear statements of what the results support | @sec-communicating |
| D. Responsibilities to research subjects and data subjects | Protect privacy and confidentiality; consider harms | @sec-deident; aggregation harm, below |
| E. Responsibilities to members of multidisciplinary teams | Respect others' expertise; make your own explicit | @sec-team-science |
| F. Responsibilities to fellow practitioners and the profession | Share methods; review fairly | @sec-communicating-review |
| G. Responsibilities of leaders, supervisors, and mentors | Foster an environment where these can be followed | Code review, @sec-git-teams |
| H. Responsibilities regarding potential misconduct | Avoid condoning it; report it through proper channels | This section |

: The eight principles of the ASA guidelines (headings
abbreviated), with where this book puts each into practice. Read
the full text; the middle column is a summary, not a quotation.
{#tbl-ethics-asa}

### Misconduct and questionable practices

**Research misconduct** has a federal definition: fabrication,
falsification, or plagiarism in proposing, performing, or reviewing
research, or in reporting its results [@ostp2000misconduct].
Fabrication is making up data or results; falsification is
manipulating materials, processes, or data, or changing or omitting
data or results, so that the research record misrepresents the
research; plagiarism is taking another's ideas, processes, results,
or words without credit. Honest error and differences of opinion
are excluded. For a statistician, the clause to remember is
'omitting data or results': dropping the patients who spoil an
estimate, without disclosure, is falsification, however it is
labeled in the code.

Between misconduct and good practice lies a wider band of
**questionable research practices** (QRPs), which surveys of
researchers find to be common [@john2012measuring]. They are rarely
fraud and frequently decisive:

| Practice | What it looks like | What prevents it |
|---|---|---|
| HARKing (hypothesizing after the results are known) | A hypothesis formed from the data presented as if stated in advance [@kerr1998harking] | A tagged analysis plan (@sec-analysis-plan) |
| Undisclosed analytic flexibility | Trying exclusions, covariates, or outcomes until one is significant [@simmons2011false] | Pre-specification; reporting every analysis run |
| Selective reporting | Publishing the outcomes or subgroups that worked | Registration; reporting against the plan |
| Optional stopping | Adding patients until p crosses 0.05 | A pre-specified sample size or stopping rule |
| Unreported exclusions | Dropping 'outliers' without a stated rule | A rule written before the data; a flow diagram |

: Questionable research practices. Each turns a nominal error rate
into an unknown one, and each is prevented by a document dated
before the data. {#tbl-ethics-qrp}

### Refusing is part of the job

There is a point at which the correct professional act is to
decline: to refuse to sign the manuscript, to refuse to produce the
figure as specified, to say that the analysis as requested is not
one you will perform. @sec-team-science distinguishes preference
from principle so that you spend your credibility on the cases
where it matters; @tbl-ethics-qrp and the five failures of this
chapter are the catalog of those cases. Principle H of the ASA
guidelines adds the harder obligation: when you suspect misconduct
by someone else, raise it through your institution's research
integrity office rather than either ignoring it or accusing anyone
in public.

### Exercises

1. Classify each as research misconduct, a questionable research
   practice, or acceptable, and say why: (a) an analyst removes
   12 patients whose outcomes 'looked wrong' and reports the
   remaining count as the sample; (b) a paper's introduction
   presents a subgroup hypothesis that the team formed after
   seeing the results; (c) an exploratory subgroup analysis is
   reported in the supplement and labeled exploratory; (d) a
   methods section copies two paragraphs from another group's
   paper without attribution.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
(a) Falsification, if the removal is undisclosed: omitting data so
that the record misrepresents the research. Disclosed, with a rule
stated before the data, it would be an exclusion open to review;
the difference is the disclosure. (b) HARKing, a QRP: the
hypothesis is presented as a priori when it was not, so the
reported p-value has no stated error rate. (c) Acceptable: the
analysis is reported and labeled for what it is
(@sec-communicating-reviewers). (d) Plagiarism, which the federal
definition names alongside fabrication and falsification; that the
copied text describes a method rather than a result does not
change it.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** Why does @tbl-ethics-qrp say each practice 'turns a
nominal error rate into an unknown one', rather than 'a false
result'?

**Answer.** Because each practice can produce a true result. What
it destroys is the ability to say how often the procedure would
produce a false one: a p-value from the fifth analysis tried is not
a 5% test, and nobody, including the analyst, can say what test it
is. The harm is to the evidence, which is why the remedy is a dated
plan rather than a better model.
:::

## Aggregation harm {#sec-ethics-aggregation}

The OkCupid release is **aggregation harm**, the same phenomenon
that @sec-deident treats formally as quasi-identifiers, arriving
from the other direction. There, no single ordinary variable
identifies anyone but their conjunction can. Here, no single
disclosure harms anyone but their conjunction can. The mathematics
is the mathematics of joint distributions; the ethics is the ethics
of context. Information carries an implicit expectation about where
it will travel, and moving it somewhere else is an act with
consequences even when every datum was freely given. Public is not
the same as consented, and available is not the same as ethical:
the question 'may I' has a legal answer and an ethical one. Ask
what happens to a person in your data if the analysis is right,
and then what happens if it is wrong.

Before you assemble a dataset from public sources, ask the three
questions in @tbl-ethics-aggregation.

| Question | Why it works | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Would the people in it be surprised? | Not 'would they object', which invites you to answer for them; surprise signals a violated contextual expectation | Users of a dating site finding their answers in a research repository |
| Does the aggregate reveal what the parts did not? | The harm is in the join, not the fields | A support-forum post linked to an employer name discloses a condition to the employer |
| Can it be de-identified without destroying the analysis? | If yes, do that (@sec-deident); if no, the identifiers are load-bearing and you should be able to say why | Usernames kept 'for linkage' that the analysis never uses |

: Three questions before assembling public data.
{#tbl-ethics-aggregation}

::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'}
> **Context.** I am considering releasing, for research, a dataset
> assembled from public profiles on a website: usernames, ages,
> locations, and answers to the site's questions. I describe the
> fields and the site's terms of use below; I attach no data.
>
> **Constraints.** Do not answer from legality alone. For each
> field and for the combination, say who the original audience
> was and who the release's audience would be.
>
> **Criteria.** Answer the three questions of a table like
> @tbl-ethics-aggregation for this dataset, name the harm a person
> in it could suffer, and say what, if anything, would make a
> release defensible.

*Failure mode.* This is the one the model will get wrong if you
let it. It reasons from legality, because legality is what is
written down, and concludes that public data may be republished;
it is agreeable, and this is the territory where an agreeable
collaborator is worse than none. The considerations exist in its
training data, but it will not volunteer them unless the prompt
forces them. *Check.* Take the question to your IRB and to a
colleague who will tell you no (@sec-ai-governance).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A colleague assembles a dataset entirely from public
sources: forum posts, a professional registry, and voter rolls. They
argue that no ethical review is needed because they disclosed
nothing new. Where does the argument fail?

**Answer.** It treats disclosure as a property of each field rather
than of the combination, and the harm is in the combination. Each
source has an implicit audience, and the people in it chose
exposure to *that* audience. Joining them creates a fact that
existed nowhere before: this named person, at this address, has
this condition. The keys that make the join possible are exactly the
quasi-identifiers of @sec-deident. 'Public' also describes access,
not permission: readable data still carry terms of use, and
scraping is a distinct act from reading. And if assembly needs no
review because each piece was public, then no aggregation ever needs
review, which nobody defends when it is stated plainly.
:::

## Causal overclaiming {#sec-ethics-causal}

The second failure is the most common in biomedical publishing, and
it usually happens in the last paragraph. An observational cohort of
self-selected volunteers reports that those who exercised more had
lower cancer incidence, adjusting for age, sex, smoking, and
body-mass index. The finding is an association. The discussion says
it 'suggests that exercise reduces cancer risk'; the press office
says exercise prevents cancer; the newspaper says it cures it. At no
step did anyone fabricate a number.

The statistician's job is to insist that the verb match the design
(Habit 11). The three registers of @sec-team-science become a
hierarchy of claims:

| Design | What you may say |
|---|---|
| Randomized, adequately powered, pre-specified | 'X reduced Y by $\delta$' |
| Observational, well adjusted, no unmeasured confounding assumed | 'X was associated with lower Y; the association is consistent with a causal effect but the design cannot establish one' |
| Observational, self-selected sample, self-reported exposure | 'Among volunteers who reported X, Y was lower. Volunteers who exercise differ from those who do not in ways we did not measure.' |

: The verb the design licenses. {#tbl-ethics-verbs}

The third row is the one to keep in view. People who exercise and
report it differ systematically from people who do not, along
dimensions (conscientiousness, health-seeking behavior, unmeasured
comorbidity, the early symptoms of undiagnosed disease) that no
covariate list captures. The adjustment cannot fix this, and
stating that you adjusted for age and smoking implies to a reader
that it did.

The transition from Results to Discussion is where the verb changes
from 'was associated with' to 'reduces' without anyone noticing.
Read your own discussion as a hostile reviewer would, and search it
for causal verbs; the search is mechanical enough to run as code.

```{r}
#| label: ethics-causal-verbs
causal_verbs <- c("reduc", "prevent", "protect", "caus", "lead",
                  "improv", "lower", "increas", "effect")

flag_causal <- function(text) {
  sentences <- unlist(strsplit(text, "(?<=\\.)\\s+", perl = TRUE))
  pattern <- paste0("\\b(", paste(causal_verbs, collapse = "|"),
                    ")[a-z]*")
  hits <- grepl(pattern, sentences, ignore.case = TRUE)
  data.frame(flagged = hits, sentence = sentences)
}

discussion <- paste(
  "Participants who exercised more had a lower incidence of cancer.",
  "This suggests that regular exercise reduces cancer risk.",
  "Physical activity may therefore protect against several cancers.",
  "The cohort was recruited from volunteers."
)
flag_causal(discussion)
```

The first flagged sentence is an association written with a
comparative ('lower'), which is fine; the second and third are
causal claims the design does not license. The search finds
candidates, and you decide; that division of labor is the right one
for a model too.

::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'}
> **Context.** Below is the discussion section of an observational
> cohort study, and one sentence describing its design (volunteer
> cohort, self-reported exposure, adjusted for age, sex, smoking,
> and body-mass index).
>
> **Constraints.** List every sentence whose verb implies
> causation. Do not rewrite the section; do not judge whether the
> causal claim is true.
>
> **Criteria.** For each sentence, quote it, name the verb, name
> the design that would license it, and propose a rewrite in the
> register of @tbl-ethics-verbs that the actual design licenses.

*Failure mode.* This works well, because it is a classification
task rather than a judgment; expect a few false positives and an
occasional miss where causation hides in a noun ('the protective
effect of exercise'). *Check.* Run `flag_causal()` on the same text
and reconcile the two lists; check each flagged sentence against
@tbl-ethics-verbs yourself.
:::

### Causal foundations

None of this means causal questions are off-limits for observational
data. Hernán argues that the euphemism is the problem: researchers
who want a causal answer but write 'associated with' have not
avoided causal inference, only hidden its assumptions from the
reader, and the remedy is to state the causal question and the
assumptions under which the analysis answers it
[@hernan2018cword]. Habit 11 and this argument agree once the
question and the verb are separated: ask the causal question
openly, and let the verb in the conclusion match what the design
and its stated assumptions support. Two tools make the assumptions
explicit.

A **directed acyclic graph** (DAG) draws the assumed causal
structure: nodes are variables, arrows are direct causal effects,
and the adjustment set a design needs can be read off the graph
[@greenland1999causal]. @fig-ethics-dag draws the exercise example.
Adjusting for age and smoking closes two backdoor paths; the path
through health-seeking behavior, which no one measured, stays open,
and that is the third row of @tbl-ethics-verbs in a picture.

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| label: fig-ethics-dag
%%| fig-alt: "Directed acyclic graph with five nodes. Exercise has an
%%|   arrow to cancer. Age, smoking, and health-seeking behavior
%%|   each have arrows to both exercise and cancer. Age and smoking
%%|   are marked as adjusted; health-seeking behavior is marked as
%%|   unmeasured."
%%| fig-cap: "A DAG for the exercise and cancer cohort. Adjustment
%%|   closes the backdoor paths through age and smoking; the path
%%|   through unmeasured health-seeking behavior remains open, so
%%|   the adjusted association is not the causal effect."
flowchart LR
  A["Age<br/><i>adjusted</i>"] --> E["Exercise"]
  S["Smoking<br/><i>adjusted</i>"] --> E
  H["Health-seeking behavior<br/><i>unmeasured</i>"] --> E
  E --> C["Cancer"]
  A --> C
  S --> C
  H --> C
```

**Target-trial emulation** asks what randomized trial you would run
if you could, and then designs the observational analysis to
emulate it, component by component: eligibility criteria, treatment
strategies, assignment, the start and end of follow-up, the outcome,
the causal contrast, and the analysis plan [@hernan2016target]. Its
most practical benefit is the alignment of time zero. Eligibility,
assignment, and the start of follow-up must coincide, as they do at
randomization. The immortal-time trap of the HF-HOME intake
(@sec-team-science), in which a patient readmitted on day 3 is
counted as unvisited, is a failure of exactly that alignment, and
writing down the target trial exposes it before any code runs.

### Exercises

2. Rewrite this paragraph from a retrospective cohort study so that
   every verb matches the design, keeping every fact: 'Patients who
   received home-health visits within a week of discharge had a
   30-day readmission rate of 18%, compared with 26% among those who
   did not (adjusted odds ratio 0.68). Home-health visits therefore
   prevent readmissions, and expanding the program would reduce
   readmissions by a third.'

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
'Patients who received a home-health visit within a week of
discharge had a lower 30-day readmission rate than those who did not
(18% versus 26%; adjusted odds ratio 0.68). Because patients
readmitted before a visit could occur are counted as unvisited, and
because visited patients may differ in ways we did not measure, this
comparison cannot establish whether the visits reduce readmission;
a randomized comparison, or an emulated trial that aligns time zero,
would be needed to estimate the effect of expanding the program.'

The changes are three. 'Prevent' becomes 'had a lower rate', the
register the design licenses. The projection ('would reduce by a
third') is removed, because it converts an association into the
effect of an intervention that was never compared. And the reason
the design falls short is named, including the immortal-time bias
specific to this comparison (@sec-team-science), which is more
useful to a reader than a generic 'causation cannot be inferred'.
Run `flag_causal()` on your rewrite: what it still flags ('lower',
'reduce') should appear only in comparative or explicitly
conditional sentences.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A colleague cites Hernán's argument to justify writing
'exercise reduces cancer risk' in the conclusion of the volunteer
cohort. What is the error?

**Answer.** The argument licenses stating the causal *question* and
its assumptions, not dropping the assumptions from the conclusion.
Here the assumption that matters, no unmeasured confounding by
health-seeking behavior, is implausible and untested, so the
honest conclusion is the causal question, the estimate under the
stated assumptions, and the reason those assumptions may fail. A
causal verb with the assumptions removed is the overclaim the
argument was meant to expose.
:::

## Visual misrepresentation {#sec-ethics-visual}

The third failure needs no numbers at all, only their encoding.
@fig-truncated plots the same two group means twice.

```{r}
#| label: fig-truncated
#| fig-cap: "The same two means, encoded twice. Panel A begins the y-axis
#|   at zero and the difference is what it is: small. Panel B begins the
#|   axis at 71 and the same difference fills the panel. Neither panel
#|   contains a false number, and a reader who glances at B carries away
#|   a conclusion the data do not support."
#| fig-alt: "Two bar panels showing the identical pair of means.
#|   In panel A the y-axis starts at zero and the two bars are
#|   almost the same height, so the difference reads as small. In
#|   panel B the y-axis starts at 71 and the same difference fills
#|   the panel, so one bar towers over the other. Only the axis
#|   limits differ between the panels."
#| fig-scap: "The same two means, encoded twice"
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)

d <- tibble(
  arm  = c("Control", "Treatment"),
  mean = c(72.4, 74.1)
)

base <- ggplot(d, aes(arm, mean, fill = arm)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Control = "#9d2235",
                               Treatment = "#1f4e79")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Score") +
  theme_minimal()

p_honest    <- base +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(title = "A. Axis from zero")

axis_floor <- 71
p_truncated <- base +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(axis_floor, 75)) +
  labs(title = paste("B. Axis from", axis_floor))

bar_ratio <- (d$mean[2] - axis_floor) / (d$mean[1] - axis_floor)

p_honest + p_truncated
```

The difference is `r round(diff(d$mean), 1)` points on a 100-point
scale. Panel A tells you that. Panel B draws the treatment bar
about `r round(bar_ratio, 1)` times as tall as the control bar,
which suggests a difference the data do not contain, without
printing a single incorrect value. The three standard distortions:

**The truncated axis.** The rule is not 'always start at zero',
because for many quantities zero is meaningless (body temperature,
calendar year, pH) and forcing it wastes the panel. The rule is that
*when the visual encoding is length or area*, as in a bar chart, the
baseline must be zero, because the reader compares lengths and a
truncated bar's length is not proportional to its value. For a
point-and-interval plot, where the encoding is position, a
truncated axis is legitimate and often necessary. The question is
always what the reader's eye is measuring.

**Area for quantity.** A map colored by which candidate won each
county encodes *land area*, and land does not vote. A bubble whose
*radius* is proportional to a count exaggerates it, because the eye
reads area, which goes as the square of the radius. In biomedicine
the recurring case is a map of disease counts that is really a map
of where people live; the fix is a rate, a denominator, and a
cartogram or population-weighted encoding.

**The dual axis.** Two series on two differently scaled y-axes can
be made to cross, converge, or diverge at the analyst's choice,
because the relative scaling is arbitrary. Avoid dual axes; to
compare two series, index them to a common baseline or use two
panels. A language model asked to critique a described figure
identifies a truncated baseline reliably and is weaker on area
encodings and denominators, which require knowing what the quantity
means; render the figure both ways, as above, and compare.

### Exercises

3. For the two means in @fig-truncated, find the axis floor at which
   the treatment bar is drawn exactly three times as tall as the
   control bar, and say what a reader would infer from that panel.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-25d-3
floor_for_ratio <- function(ratio, low, high) {
  (ratio * low - high) / (ratio - 1)
}
floor_3 <- floor_for_ratio(3, d$mean[1], d$mean[2])
c(floor = floor_3,
  check = (d$mean[2] - floor_3) / (d$mean[1] - floor_3))
```

Setting $(74.1 - f) = 3(72.4 - f)$ gives
$f = `r round(floor_3, 2)`$. A reader of that panel would infer that
treatment roughly triples the score, from a difference of
`r round(diff(d$mean), 1)` points on a 100-point scale. The floor
needed is only about a point below the control mean, which is how
easily a default axis range produces the distortion.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A forest plot of hazard ratios uses a horizontal axis
from 0.5 to 2, not from zero. Is that a truncated-axis distortion?

**Answer.** No. The encoding is position, not length: each estimate
is a point with an interval, and the reader compares positions
against the reference line at 1. Starting at zero would waste the
panel and compress the intervals. (A log scale is also the right
choice for ratios, so that 0.5 and 2 sit equally far from 1.)
:::

## The overlapping-interval fallacy {#sec-ethics-overlap}

The fourth failure is the one a biostatistician is most likely to
commit personally, and it is a technical error rather than a
rhetorical one. The reasoning goes: the 95% confidence intervals for
the two group means overlap, therefore the difference is not
significant at the 5% level. This is wrong, and wrong in the
direction of missing real effects. The interval for a *difference*
depends on the standard error of the difference, which is smaller
than the sum of the two individual standard errors, so intervals for
the two means can overlap while the interval for their difference
excludes zero. A demonstration, on synthetic data constructed to
make the point sharply:

```{r}
#| label: overlap-demo
set.seed(18)

a <- rnorm(60, mean = 100, sd = 12)
b <- rnorm(60, mean = 105, sd = 12)

ci <- function(x) {
  m  <- mean(x)
  se <- sd(x) / sqrt(length(x))
  c(lower = m - 1.96 * se, mean = m, upper = m + 1.96 * se)
}

ci_tab <- rbind(group_a = ci(a), group_b = ci(b)) |> round(1)
ci_tab

overlap_test <- t.test(b, a)
overlap_test
```

The two intervals overlap: group A reaches
`r ci_tab["group_a", "upper"]` and group B begins at
`r ci_tab["group_b", "lower"]`. The two-sample test nonetheless
rejects at the 5% level
($p = `r round(overlap_test$p.value, 2)`$). Anyone reading the
overlap off a figure and concluding 'no significant difference' has
reached the opposite conclusion from the one the data support.

The overlap here is about
`r round(ci_tab["group_a", "upper"] - ci_tab["group_b", "lower"], 1)`
point, which is deliberate: the fallacy does its damage in exactly
this regime, where the intervals graze each other and the difference
is real. As the difference grows the intervals separate and the two
readings agree; as it shrinks the test stops rejecting and they agree
again. It is the middle, where an analyst most wants guidance from
the figure, that the heuristic gets wrong. @fig-overlap shows the
correct object: the interval for the difference, which answers the
question actually asked.

```{r}
#| label: fig-overlap
#| fig-cap: "Left: the two group means with their 95% intervals, which
#|   overlap. Right: the 95% interval for the difference, which excludes
#|   zero. These are not in conflict; they are answers to different
#|   questions. Reading significance off the overlap on the left is the
#|   error."
#| fig-alt: "Two panels. On the left, two group means each with a
#|   95 percent confidence interval; the two intervals visibly
#|   overlap. On the right, a single 95 percent interval for the
#|   difference between the means, plotted against a reference line
#|   at zero, which it clearly excludes."
#| fig-scap: "Overlapping intervals versus the interval for the difference"
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.2
means <- bind_rows(
  as_tibble_row(ci(a)) |> mutate(group = "A"),
  as_tibble_row(ci(b)) |> mutate(group = "B")
)

tt <- t.test(b, a)
diff <- tibble(
  group = "B - A",
  mean  = unname(diff(rev(tt$estimate))),
  lower = tt$conf.int[1],
  upper = tt$conf.int[2]
)

p_means <- ggplot(means, aes(mean, group)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = lower, xmax = upper)) +
  labs(title = "A. Group means", x = "Score", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

p_diff <- ggplot(diff, aes(mean, group)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = lower, xmax = upper)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "#9d2235") +
  labs(title = "B. Difference", x = "Difference in score",
       y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

p_means + p_diff
```

The practical consequences are two. When you *report*, give the
interval for the contrast, not merely intervals for the arms,
because the contrast is the estimand. When you *review*, treat any
sentence of the form 'the intervals overlapped, so the groups did
not differ' as an error, and say so.

### Exercises

4. Construct a dataset in which two group means have overlapping
   95% intervals and a two-sample t-test rejects at the 5% level.
   State the largest overlap you can achieve while retaining
   significance, and explain the relationship between the standard
   error of a mean and the standard error of a difference.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
Build the groups deterministically rather than by sampling, so that
the demonstration does not depend on the draw. Standardizing a
random vector gives a group with exactly the mean and standard
deviation you asked for:

```{r}
#| label: soln-25d-1
set.seed(21)
n <- 60
exact <- function(mean, sd, n) {
  z <- as.numeric(scale(rnorm(n)))   # mean 0, sd 1 exactly
  mean + sd * z
}

g1 <- exact(100.00, 6, n)
g2 <- exact(102.63, 6, n)            # delta chosen below

ci <- function(x) mean(x) + c(-1, 1) * qt(0.975, length(x) - 1) *
                  sd(x) / sqrt(length(x))

round(ci(g1), 2)
round(ci(g2), 2)

tt <- t.test(g2, g1)
round(c(difference = mean(g2) - mean(g1),
        p = tt$p.value), 4)
round(as.numeric(tt$conf.int), 2)
```

The two per-group intervals overlap, the test rejects, and the
interval for the difference excludes zero. Nothing here is
contradictory; the three statements answer different questions.

The arithmetic is the whole explanation, and it sets the window the
delta above was chosen from. The standard error of one mean is
$s/\sqrt{n}$. The standard error of the *difference* of two
independent means is $\sqrt{s_1^2/n_1 + s_2^2/n_2}$, which for equal
groups is $\sqrt{2}$ times one group's standard error, not twice it.
Writing $c \approx 2$ for the critical value at $n = 60$:

- The two intervals **overlap** while
  $\delta < 2c\,s/\sqrt{n} \approx 4.0\,s/\sqrt{n}$.
- The test **rejects** once
  $\delta > c\sqrt{2}\,s/\sqrt{n} \approx 2.83\,s/\sqrt{n}$.

Any $\delta$ between those two bounds gives both at once, and with
$s = 6$ and $n = 60$ the window is roughly 2.19 to 3.10. The value
2.63 sits in the middle of it.

**The largest overlap you can achieve** is at the lower edge, where
the test only just rejects:

```{r}
#| label: soln-25d-1b
overlap_at <- function(delta, n = 60, sd = 6) {
  set.seed(21)
  a <- exact(100, sd, n); b <- exact(100 + delta, sd, n)
  ca <- ci(a); cb <- ci(b)
  c(delta = delta,
    p = t.test(b, a)$p.value,
    overlap = unname(ca[2] - cb[1]))
}

sweep <- t(vapply(c(2.2, 2.4, 2.63, 2.8, 3.0, 3.2),
                  overlap_at, numeric(3))) |>
  round(3)
sweep
```

Every row here rejects, so read the *first*: at
$\delta = `r sweep[1, "delta"]`$ the test gives
$p = `r sweep[1, "p"]`$ and the intervals still overlap by
`r round(sweep[1, "overlap"], 2)` units, which is the widest overlap
compatible with significance in this design. Reducing $\delta$
further loses the rejection. Going the other way, the overlap
shrinks steadily and turns negative by
$\delta = `r sweep[nrow(sweep), "delta"]`$, where the intervals
have separated. The sweep also confirms the bounds computed above:
the lower edge sits just under 2.2 and the upper just over 3.0,
against the predicted 2.19 and 3.10.

Reading significance off the overlap on the left-hand panel of
@fig-overlap is therefore not a conservative approximation. It is a
test with the wrong standard error, and it fails in the direction of
declaring 'no difference' when there is one.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** Two arms' 95% intervals do *not* overlap. May you
conclude that the difference is significant at the 5% level?

**Answer.** Yes, for two independent estimates: non-overlap is a
stricter criterion than the test, so it errs only toward missing
real differences, never toward declaring false ones. The fallacy runs
one way only, which is why it hides: the rule 'overlap means no
difference' sounds like the mirror image of a correct rule and is
not.
:::

## Unrepresentative samples {#sec-ethics-representation}

The fifth failure is the one whose costs fall on people who are not
in the room, and often not in the data. It is the failure of **fair
representation**, and it is why a competent statistician asks who a
sample contains before, not after, generalizing from it. The
falsehood, once again, is in no number; it is in the silent step
from 'this holds in the sample' to 'this holds', taken when the
sample and the target are not the same population and no one has
said so. This book's own source material shows the mechanism: the
survey behind the team-science reading drew respondents who were
82.8% White, and its authors state plainly that their conclusions
may not transport to a more diverse workforce [@slade2023team]. The
honesty is the model; the skew is the hazard.

**A sample is evidence about the population it was drawn from, and
no other.** A drug trial that enrolls at academic medical centers,
among patients who can attend visits every two weeks, skews toward
the younger, the insured, the urban, and those without other
illnesses. Applied to the older, rural, multiply morbid patient to
whom the drug will be prescribed, its estimate is an extrapolation
[@rothwell2005external]. Adjusting for age does not repair this, for
the reason it did not repair the volunteer cohort: the groups differ
along dimensions no covariate list enumerates.

**Under-representation is a bias-and-variance problem with a face.**
When a subgroup is a small fraction of the sample, its estimate is
imprecise, so an effect specific to them is the effect you are least
able to detect; and if the effect genuinely differs there, the pooled
estimate, dominated by the majority, is biased for them. A result
reported as though it applied to everyone fails exactly the people
the sample underweighted, and fails them silently, because the
interval on the pooled estimate looks reassuringly tight.

**A model learns the sample's inequities and returns them as
findings.** Where an analysis feeds a decision rule (a risk score, an
eligibility threshold, a resource-allocation model), a biased
training sample propagates the bias at scale. The canonical case is
a health-system algorithm that used prior health-care spending as a
proxy for health need and, because less had historically been spent
on Black patients at equal levels of illness, systematically
understated their need [@obermeyer2019dissecting]. Every number was
correctly computed. The proxy was the error, and only someone asking
what the variable *stood for* could have caught it.

The discipline is cheap, and @tbl-ethics-representation lists it.

| Practice | What to do | Example sentence or check |
|---|---|---|
| Report who is in the sample beside who the result is for | Table 1 by demographic group; name the populations to which the estimate does and does not transport | 'Our cohort was 91% White and privately insured; generalization to other populations is unestablished.' |
| Pre-specify the subgroups you are powered to examine | Label the rest exploratory (@sec-analysis-plan) | A subgroup you were not powered for yields an imprecise estimate, not an absence of effect |
| Ask what a decision variable is a proxy for | Before a predictor enters a model that acts on people, check whether it encodes a protected characteristic and whether errors are borne equally | Spending as a proxy for need |
| Make the artifact readable by every reader | Color-blind-safe palettes, verified before publication (@sec-graphics) | Red versus green is illegible to roughly 8% of men |

: Representation checks, from sample to artifact. A result that
reaches only some of its readers, or speaks for only some of its
subjects, is not the finished product it looks like.
{#tbl-ethics-representation}

::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'}
**A subgroup row in Table 1 is reported; its uncertainty is not.**
A Table 1 that lists a few dozen patients in a group invites a
reader to treat the group as studied. A subgroup estimate for a few
dozen patients has an interval so wide that it can neither show nor exclude any
plausible effect, and a report that says 'no difference was observed
in this group' has converted imprecision into a finding. Report the
interval, or say that the group was too small to examine.
:::

### Exercises

5. Using the HF-HOME files, compute for each race category the
   number of randomized patients and the half-width of the 95%
   interval for the risk difference between arms among ascertained
   patients. Which groups could support any subgroup claim?

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-25d-5
hf_dir <- file.path("..", "data", "raw_data", "hfhome")
read_hf <- function(file) {
  read_csv(file.path(hf_dir, file),
           col_types = cols(patient_id = "c", .default = "?"))
}

hf <- read_hf("randomization.csv") |>
  select(patient_id, arm) |>
  left_join(read_hf("outcomes.csv") |>
              select(patient_id, ascertained, event_30d),
            by = "patient_id", relationship = "one-to-one",
            unmatched = "error") |>
  left_join(read_hf("demographics.csv") |> select(patient_id, race),
            by = "patient_id", relationship = "one-to-one",
            unmatched = "error")
stopifnot(nrow(hf) == nrow(read_hf("randomization.csv")))

by_race <- hf |>
  filter(ascertained) |>
  group_by(race, arm) |>
  summarize(n = n(), p = mean(event_30d), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(race) |>
  summarize(patients = sum(n),
            half_width = 100 * qnorm(0.975) *
              sqrt(sum(p * (1 - p) / n)),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(patients)
by_race
```

The smallest groups have half-widths of about
`r round(max(by_race$half_width))` points, against an overall effect
of a few points: they can support no subgroup claim at all, in
either direction. Only the largest group,
`r by_race$race[nrow(by_race)]`, has a half-width
(`r round(by_race$half_width[nrow(by_race)], 1)` points) below the
5-point reduction the trial was designed to detect, and only just,
because it holds about half the trial. The honest
report gives the composition, says that the trial was not designed to
estimate effects by race, and names the groups too small to examine,
rather than reporting 'no difference' in each.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A risk model is trained on a health system's records
and validated with excellent overall discrimination. What question
does the overall validation leave unanswered?

**Answer.** Whether the model's errors are borne equally. Overall
discrimination is dominated by the majority of the sample, and a
model can rank well overall while systematically under- or
over-predicting for a group, especially if a predictor is a proxy
for something other than what it is named for. Validate by group,
and ask what each predictor stands for, before the model acts on
anyone.
:::

## Rules of thumb

1. **Habit 11: lead with the answer, and match the verb to the
   design.** Observational studies license association; when the
   question is causal, state it and its assumptions openly.
2. **Habit 5: pre-specify, then tag.** A dated plan is what
   separates a reported exploratory analysis from HARKing, and a
   powered subgroup from an imprecise one.
3. **Habit 8: a bug that produces a plausible number is the
   expensive kind.** A truncated axis, an overlap read as a test,
   and a proxy variable all produce plausible pictures; ask what the
   reader's eye, the test, and the variable are measuring.

## Cumulative practice

6. *Cumulative (uses @sec-graphics and @sec-communicating).* Draw
   HF-HOME's primary result twice: once as two bars of observed
   risk with the y-axis from 20% to 24.5% and no intervals, and once
   as the risk difference with its 95% interval against zero and the
   5-point minimum clinically important difference. Write one
   sentence a reader would take from each.
7. *On your own work (no key).* Take the discussion section of a
   paper you have co-authored. Run `flag_causal()` on it, then, for
   every flagged sentence, state the design that would license it
   and the design you actually had, and rewrite any that fail.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution to exercise 6'}
```{r}
#| label: fig-soln-25d-6
#| fig-cap: "HF-HOME's primary result drawn twice. Left: observed
#|   risks as bars on a truncated axis, with no intervals. Right: the
#|   risk difference with its 95% interval, against zero (solid) and
#|   the 5-point MCID (dashed)."
#| fig-alt: "Two panels. On the left, two bars on an axis from 20 to
#|   24.5 percent; the usual-care bar is much taller than the
#|   home-health bar. On the right, a single point with a horizontal
#|   interval that crosses a solid line at zero and extends past a
#|   dashed line at 5."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3
arm_risk <- hf |>
  filter(ascertained) |>
  group_by(arm) |>
  summarize(n = n(), risk = mean(event_30d), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(arm = factor(arm, levels = c("Usual care", "Home health"))) |>
  arrange(arm)

rd <- 100 * (arm_risk$risk[1] - arm_risk$risk[2])
se <- 100 * sqrt(sum(arm_risk$risk * (1 - arm_risk$risk) / arm_risk$n))
rd_tab <- tibble(label = "Usual care minus home health", est = rd,
                 lower = rd - qnorm(0.975) * se,
                 upper = rd + qnorm(0.975) * se)

p_bad <- ggplot(arm_risk, aes(arm, 100 * risk)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(20, 24.5)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "30-day risk (%)",
       title = "A. Home health works?") +
  theme_minimal()

p_good <- ggplot(rd_tab, aes(est, label)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 5, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = lower, xmax = upper)) +
  labs(x = "Risk difference (points)", y = NULL,
       title = "B. Inconclusive") +
  theme_minimal()

p_bad + p_good
```

Panel A says 'home health cut readmissions sharply'; panel B says
'the trial cannot distinguish no effect from a reduction of about
`r round(rd_tab$upper)` points'. Both use the same
`r format(sum(arm_risk$n), big.mark = ",")` ascertained patients and
print no false number. Panel A commits two of this chapter's
failures at once: a truncated length encoding, and a pair of arm
estimates shown without the contrast that is the estimand.
:::

## Cheat sheet

| Failure | Ask | Do |
|---|---|---|
| Aggregation harm | Would the people in it be surprised? | De-identify, or do not assemble |
| Misconduct and QRPs | Was this decision dated before the data? | Pre-specify; disclose every exclusion and analysis |
| Causal overclaiming | Does the design license the verb? | Rewrite to the licensed register; state causal assumptions openly |
| Visual misrepresentation | What is the reader's eye measuring? | Zero baseline for length; no dual axes |
| Overlapping intervals | Is the claim about the contrast? | Report and plot the interval for the difference |
| Unrepresentative sample | To whom does the estimate transport? | Report composition; name the populations it does not cover |

: Ethics beyond compliance at a glance. {#tbl-ethics-cheat-sheet}

- [@asa2022ethical], the profession's own statement of what this
  chapter argues, and the document to cite when you decline.
- [@hernan2018cword], on stating causal questions openly rather than
  hiding them behind associational language.
- [@obermeyer2019dissecting], the health-system algorithm whose
  proxy variable encoded and propagated racial bias at scale.

## Prerequisites answers {#sec-quiz-answers-25d}

1. Because the harm of aggregation differs from the harm of
   disclosure. Each individual disclosed a fact to an audience of
   their choosing, in a context they understood; assembling those
   disclosures into a single searchable, permanent, downloadable
   artifact and attaching identifiers to it does something none of
   them chose. The aggregate can reveal what no individual datum
   did, for example by linking a health disclosure in one forum to
   an employer named in another. This is the joint-distribution
   phenomenon that makes quasi-identifiers dangerous in
   @sec-deident, arriving from the other direction. The test is not
   'was each item public' but 'would the people in the dataset be
   surprised to find themselves in it'.
2. No. The confidence interval for the *difference* depends on the
   standard error of the difference, which is smaller than the sum
   of the two individual standard errors, so two means can have
   overlapping intervals while the interval for their difference
   excludes zero and the two-sample test rejects. The error runs in
   the direction of missing real effects. Report and inspect the
   interval for the contrast, which is the estimand.
3. (Any three of:) a truncated axis on a length-encoded chart, so
   that a 1.7-point difference on a 100-point scale fills the panel;
   encoding a quantity as area, including a map colored by land
   rather than by population, or a bubble whose radius rather than
   area is proportional to the count; a dual axis, whose relative
   scaling is an arbitrary choice that can make two series appear to
   converge or diverge; omitting the uncertainty, so that a point
   estimate invites more confidence than it has earned; and choosing
   a denominator that flatters the conclusion. None requires
   printing a false number.
